prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and for its experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from dynamical mean-field theory (B005) to the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulator (B012). The round-1 exchange did not give me a new argument for the physics of DMFT, which I still consider mature and important, but it showed that I am the only member holding it, that four colleagues independently put the attribution problem in the same place I did (Metzner, Muller-Hartmann and Jarrell outside the trio), and that nobody, including me, can describe a fair three-name prize. I said in round 1 that if no fair prize can be built the committee should look elsewhere, and I should apply that to my own first choice instead of defending it out of field loyalty. B012 is where I would look. Kane and Mele made the conceptual step: a Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant band insulators, with helical edge states that are protected and not accidental. Molenkamp's group then measured quantized edge conduction in HgTe wells, which is the kind of concrete, reproducible observation the statute asks for. For more than fifteen years it has been checked by transport, ARPES and STM in several materials, so, unlike the moire case, the interpretation is stable. Seven of eight members ranked it in the opening round and all seven proposed the same trio, which is not a substitute for scientific judgment, but it does mean the credit question has been looked at by many people independently and given the same answer. As a first-principles theorist I also note that the band-inversion mechanism in HgTe and the later materials predictions were computed with the electronic-structure methods I work with, and that spin-orbit-driven band inversion is exactly the sort of effect those calculations can test quantitatively.
statement.case_against: The attribution is incomplete and I will not pretend otherwise. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe quantum-well proposal that Molenkamp's experiment tested, Zhang is deceased, and the three-dimensional topological-insulator stream (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents; Hsieh, Hasan) is a separate credit line that this configuration leaves out. The citation therefore has to be worded narrowly around the two-dimensional Z2 insulator and its observation, and I do not think it can honestly be worded as a prize for topological insulators in general. The 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and topological phases is a real overlap in subject, although I read the Z2 invariant with time-reversal-protected edge states as a distinct and later advance, and the committee should be able to explain that distinction in a sentence. Finally, the practical payoff of quantum spin Hall edge channels is limited because edge conduction in real samples is imperfect. I also note that my first choice is now off the table only because of my own attribution objection; I have not stopped believing in DMFT.

responses.point: Pearce argued that the 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions and integer quantum Hall-type phases, whereas the Z2 invariant and time-reversal-protected edge states are a separate, later discovery with its own experimental verification, and that no cleaner three-name split exists in this topic.
responses.response: I accept this distinction and it is the main reason I have moved. Time-reversal symmetry and the Z2 invariant are not a repackaging of the Chern-number classification, and the edge states in the HgTe wells are not protected by a magnetic-field-induced gap. Where I would push back is on your point that there is no cleaner split. The same argument could be made about DMFT, where I could not find one either, and I gave that up. The difference I now see is that for B012 the trio has an identifiable theory-then-measurement structure, and the missing names are a well-defined set (the BHZ proposal and the 3D work) that a narrowly worded citation can stay clear of. I would ask that we draft the citation around the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect so that it does not imply recognition of the whole topological-insulator field.

responses.point: Johansson moved from circuit QED to B012, calling it the candidate with the broadest and most robust support, a distinct advance from the 2016 prize, and timely to somewhat overdue, while accepting that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang attribution is the real weakness.
responses.response: I agree on the weakness and on the maturity, and I take your point that B012 has a concrete experimental observation behind the theory, which is what I failed to give weight to in my own method-versus-discovery argument. I would qualify the claim that real-material edge conduction is a minor limitation. In HgTe the quantized conductance is clean only in short edges, which is something Molenkamp's group itself reported, and the committee should not let the citation imply that dissipationless edge transport has been demonstrated at length scales relevant to applications. That would be an overstatement of the discovery. It does not change my view that the observation is real and reproduced. I also note your candour about circuit QED and your recusal advice; I share your reluctance to see a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025.

responses.point: Danielsson defended B047 as a sharp quantitative prediction followed by a reproduced discovery, argued that the unsettled superconducting mechanism concerns interpretation and not whether the discovery is real, and rejected a two-person prize because Bistritzer is the first author of the 2011 magic-angle calculation.
responses.response: You have changed my view on one point and not on another. On credit, I now agree that dropping Bistritzer would credit a calculation by two authors to one, and I withdraw my suggestion of a two-name prize, although I would still say the experimental credit (Cao, Fatemi and the parallel moire work) is thinner than for B012. On timing, the high-Tc comparison is fair as far as it goes, but there the discovery itself was a bulk property that many groups measured identically. In twisted bilayer graphene the phase diagram depends on twist-angle disorder and sample preparation, so even the list of observed phases varies between devices. I therefore still put B047 below B012 this year, but I would put it first among the alternatives and I would expect it to overtake B012 within a few years if the device-to-device variability is brought under control.

responses.point: Lindroth argued that the optical lattice clock has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, with two names and measurable performance, and that she would not oppose B005 if a defensible triple were found but does not think it is stronger on attribution.
responses.response: On attribution you are right and I concede it for B005. I do not agree that cleaner attribution alone makes B019 the better prize. A committee that treats the 2005 and 2012 prizes as context and not as a bar needs a reason why the lattice clock is a new principle and not a continuation, and your own uncertainty list says the answer depends on how the citation is drafted. Atomic physics is outside my field and I cannot adjudicate Katori's priority against Lemonde, so I leave that to you and Kroll. What I would ask is whether the case for the clock rests on the invention of magic-wavelength trapping or on the 10^-18 accuracy reached afterwards, because a citation for the second would be a prize for engineering excellence, and the first would be a narrower claim.

responses.point: Kroll kept B019 first and said he would hold DMFT in reserve, noting that I had not verified the priority split between the infinite-dimension limit and the impurity-model mapping and that usefulness should not be equated with discovery.
responses.response: The criticism is fair, and I have acted on it by moving off B005. I did not get the priority split verified, and I should not ask colleagues to carry a configuration whose key attribution question I could not resolve. I disagree only with the implication that a framework tested against experiment cannot qualify; the point I would keep for the record is that the DMFT spectral and thermodynamic predictions were checked against data. For the lattice clock I would add one practical test: if the second is redefined in the coming years on the basis of these clocks, the prize will look timely, and if not, the committee loses nothing by waiting, because there is no competing claim that would erode the credit in the meantime.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from active matter to B047, stressing that a single control parameter, the twist angle, turns correlation strength into a laboratory variable, and said that if the committee wants settled interpretation then B012 is clearly the more mature choice.
responses.response: Your last sentence is the one I agree with most, and I have followed it. I would add a physical caution to the twist-angle argument: the angle is a control parameter, but the effective angle varies across a device by tenths of a degree, and near the magic angle the flat-band width is so sensitive to this that comparison with theory is not yet quantitative. That is a materials-quality issue and not a flaw in the discovery, so I do not treat it as disqualifying. It is why I rank B047 as the leading alternative and not as my preferred part, and the choice between them is about timing and not about whether either is real physics.

uncertainties: Whether a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp citation can be worded narrowly enough, around the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and its observation, that it does not misstate how the field arose or ignore the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal.
Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize is only context or a real bar for a closely related topic; I judge it context, but I am not certain the whole committee will.
Whether the 3D topological-insulator contributors (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents; Hsieh, Hasan) would be reasonably held outside a prize that is explicitly about the two-dimensional effect.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene will become stable enough in interpretation and device reproducibility to overtake B012 within a few years.
Whether my own turn away from DMFT is influenced by seeing no support for it, and whether my remaining view of its importance is biased by my own methodological work.
statement.conflict_note: No personal connection to any credited candidate is documented in my profile, and none of Kane, Mele or Molenkamp is a known co-author, collaborator or institutional colleague. I do work with density functional theory and dynamical mean-field methods, so I disclosed a field-proximity bias for B005 in round 1; that is no longer my preferred part, but it still applies to B005 as an alternative and the committee should discount my view of it. Electronic-structure calculations of band inversion in topological materials are close to my own methods, which is a field proximity for B012 but not a personal or institutional tie. My documented ties (Borje Johansson, Los Alamos, co-authors of my books and Uppsala colleagues) do not link to any shortlisted candidate as far as the provided profile shows.
